reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .411 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.70 xERA on the mound — pick one, either profile alone would anchor a roster. The bat gets there through a 15.2% walk rate and a 16.5% barrel rate working together, a patient approach married to elite contact quality; the 22.8% strikeout rate is the only real cost, and it's a price most teams would pay twice. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball spinning at 2486 rpm suppresses barrels to 3.8% and drives a 30.4% whiff rate, which is what a 2.70 xERA looks like before you've even seen the results. The projection of .283/.397/.546 with 38 home runs across 687 plate appearances is just the hitting half, and the honest floor here is a two-way contributor who happens to be doing things no actuarial table has priced before.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six home runs at 22 years old is a number that demands a reason, and the Statcast profile supplies one: 93.1 mph average exit velocity, a 51.5% hard-hit rate, and a .371 xwOBA that all sit in the same tier, confirming the power isn't a quirk of batted-ball luck. The walk rate at 12.3% is the quiet piece, separating a true middle-of-the-order bat from a hitter you can pitch around, and it combines with an 18.3% strikeout rate to produce a contact-and-discipline profile that makes a .275/.356/.542 projection feel like a floor, not a ceiling. The fielding is genuinely bad, the kind of OAA percentile that will eventually force the conversation about where he plays long-term. But if the plate discipline holds at its current shape, Caminero is a franchise corner hitter, and the rest is a roster-construction problem.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .312, 100th percentile, tells you the contact quality is already doing things his current .290 projection doesn't fully capture. Witt's Statcast profile is a study in how far elite physicality can carry a player past his discipline: 93.3 mph average exit velocity and 53.0% hard-hit rate pair with a chase rate sitting in just the 30th percentile, and he still gets to a 16.7% strikeout rate because he makes hard contact when he does swing. Add 30.3 ft/s sprint speed at the 99th percentile and the projected 46 steals aren't a luxury, they're load-bearing. If the chase rate ever tightens and the walk rate climbs past 10.0%, the .393 xwOBA profile stops looking like a ceiling and starts looking like a floor.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: A 22.8% barrel rate and a 17.5% walk rate on the same card is the argument, full stop. The contact limits are genuine: pitchers are beating him inside the zone, not outside it, because a 31.1% whiff rate sits against a 22.4% chase rate. But when Wood makes contact, the .615 xSLG says what kind of contact it is. If pitchers find the in-zone sequence that exposes the whiff rate at scale, the projection's .265/.389/.523 line compresses; if the 17.5% walk rate holds, he has enough margin to absorb a 28.9% strikeout rate and still be a middle-of-the-order force at 23.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA sits at .367 and the hard-hit rate at 49.2%, so the bat is doing genuine damage when it connects — the tension is that a 35.9% chase rate keeps the strikeouts at 25.5% and caps how often he actually connects. The speed is elite, 29.4 ft/s, and it inflates everything: the batting average, the stolen base totals, the run-scoring value of balls in play that would be outs for a slower player. If the chase rate doesn't come down, the projection's .279 AVG and .871 OPS require the speed to keep doing heavy lifting, and a slight decline in either contact or legs makes this profile look a lot thinner. When it holds, though, 33 home runs and 38 stolen bases at 24 years old is a legitimate star season.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the one jagged edge in an otherwise elite profile. Kurtz's 58.3% hard-hit rate and 18.4% walk rate are both genuinely rare, and the .379 xwOBA reflects a hitter who does serious damage when he connects. The problem is a 36.8% whiff rate that sits near the bottom of the league, and whether those two things can coexist at scale is the whole argument. The projection says they can, landing at .263/.394/.505 with 36 projected home runs, essentially betting that the walk rate and raw power are loud enough to carry the strikeouts — and the xSLG of .493 suggests the batted-ball shape backs that up. If the whiff rate doesn't soften as he sees more big-league looks, the average erodes and the profile slides from star to streaky slugger; if it does, you have a middle-of-the-order first baseman with an uncommon combination of patience and thump.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.74 and the ERA projection comes in at 3.32, and the gap between those two numbers is where the whole argument lives. Skenes misses bats at a 29.3% clip while walking just 5.5%, a combination that makes the contact management almost secondary — the xwOBA against is .259, and hitters simply aren't squaring him up with enough frequency to matter. The whiff rate (27.8%) and chase rate (33.5%) are good rather than elite, which means the strikeout volume is built on the walk suppression as much as pure swing-and-miss; if the command slips, the strikeout total softens before anything else does. At 23 and projecting for 181.7 innings at a 1.06 WHIP, he's already a mid-rotation anchor at his floor and a genuine ace if the peripherals hold.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.peak_summary: Projection: impact everyday bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is impact over 232 PA.
reports.published_report: The .417 OBP is the skeleton of this profile, and at 18, it doesn't look like a fluke of circumstance — 62 walks in 343 plate appearances at A+/A is a plate discipline shape that scouts don't often see this young. Willits is also hitting .279 with a .215 ISO and 38 stolen bases, which means the approach isn't buying time for a player who can't do anything else. The MLB-equivalent translation discounts the walk rate to 12.2%, well clear of the 8.5% MLB average, but the power shrinks to a .141 ISO where the MLB average sits at .150, which means the ceiling rests on the bat speed and hit tool maturing alongside the approach rather than on power he's already showing. If the hit and power grades get to the 65s projected here, you have an impact everyday shortstop in two to three years; if the bat doesn't carry against upper-minors velocity, the approach alone profiles as a bench piece with patience and speed.

If he does, the ceiling is a mid-rotation starter or better, and the floor is a multi-inning arm who still beats most MLB rosters.

He won't beat you on the bases and the glove is average, so this profile lives entirely in the box, where it is about as clean as hitting gets right now.

reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud — 12.1 K/9 at AA, translating to 9.3 against major-league hitters, which sits above a league average of 8.6, but the walks are eating the profile alive. reports.name: Kyle Tucker
reports.published_report: Tucker's Statcast profile tells a story that doesn't quite match the reputation: a 5.3% barrel rate and 38.6% hard-hit rate are solidly below average for a middle-of-the-order bat, and the .385 xSLG is the quiet confession that the power hasn't translated the way people remember. What carries the profile is discipline — a 13.0% walk rate that puts him well into the top tier of the league, and a 24.8% chase rate that keeps him in counts where he can do damage even without elite exit velocity. The projection lands at .253/.355/.414, and that OBP holds up because the walk rate is backed by a chase rate in the 78th percentile; the 18 projected home runs are what you get when contact quality is ordinary but the plate approach is genuinely elite. If the hip limits him further and the walk rate erodes, this is a league-average outfielder on a big contract; if the discipline holds and the exit velo recovers even modestly, he's a useful regular who earns his lineup spot a different way than he used to.

reports.published_report:
The strikeout rate and walk rate look like a mid-rotation starter. The contact profile doesn't.

reports.name: Carlos Lagrange
reports.peak_summary: Projection: multi-inning or setup reliever with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 63.3 IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the argument for Lagrange, and the walk rate is the argument against him. Across 63.3 innings at AAA, he's punching out 11.8 per nine while issuing 4.7 walks per nine, and when you translate that to a major-league context the picture sharpens only slightly: a 9.6 K/9 against a 4.2 BB/9, with a K-BB% of 13.9% that's basically at the MLB mean. The miss grades at 65 on the skill shape, command sits at 35, and those two numbers together explain why a move to shorter stints isn't a downgrade so much as a structural fix. If the walks tighten in a multi-inning or setup role, he's a useful major-league arm; if they don't, he's organizational depth.

reports.published_report: Nineteen home runs and a .390 OBP from a 20-year-old catcher in AA is the kind of profile that stops conversations. The ISO translates to .171 in MLB-equivalent terms, above a league norm of .150, and the walk rate clears 11.8% against a major-league average of 8.5%, which means the power isn't coming at the expense of the zone. The strikeout rate is the one honest flag: 28.2% in translation, well above the MLB mean of 22.0%, and whether Alfredo Duno becomes a regular at the position hinges almost entirely on whether that number bends as pitching gets sharper. If it does, a low-end everyday catcher is a realistic outcome within a year or two; if it doesn't, he's a reserve with loud tools and limited at-bat quality.

reports.name: Mookie Betts
reports.published_report: The contact grades are still elite — a 19.6% chase rate and 12.6% whiff rate both sit at the 96th percentile or better, but the power side has quietly softened, and that gap between plate discipline and damage numbers is where this profile gets complicated. His xBA of .280 says he's making excellent contact, yet 40.0% hard-hit and an 8.5% barrel rate land below the median in raw power production, which is why the projection settles at .254/.326/.445 rather than anything that recalls his peak. The walk rate at 7.6% is modest for a hitter whose zone control is this good, suggesting pitchers have found that working edges without expanding is viable when the barrel percentage doesn't punish them for it. If the hard-hit rate trends upward, the .445 SLG becomes a floor; if it stays where it is, you're looking at a very good contact hitter with second-division regular power, still useful on a contender, just not the runaway value he once was.

reports.name: Freddy Peralta
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a puzzle: a 3.75 xERA with contact quality that looks genuinely suppressed, built almost entirely on spin rather than velocity. His barrel rate sits at 5.0% and average exit velocity at 87.8 mph, both comfortably better than league average, and 2422 rpm on the fastball explains how a 94.1 mph heater still generates weak contact. The strikeout rate at 22.0% and chase rate at 29.2% are both below average, meaning he's not missing bats at volume — he's winning by limiting damage when contact happens. That's a fragile blueprint: if the spin-driven soft contact dries up, a 4.37 ERA projection with a 1.36 WHIP and only 10 quality starts becomes the floor, not a conservative estimate. He profiles as a back-end starter who earns his keep through contact management, and the honest ceiling is a mid-rotation arm if the walk rate (8.8%) ever tightens.

reports.published_report: The xERA and xwOBA both sit at the 96th percentile, and the gap between those marks and a 3.16 projected ERA tells you the current-year number is already being conservative. Megill's 36.4% chase rate and 31.7% strikeout rate drive the profile — hitters are swinging at his stuff out of the zone and missing it when they do connect, and the 2.49 xERA reflects what happens when that combination holds.
